content.abstract:
Fifteenth Indian Expedition to Antarctica, Scientific Report. 1999 
Department of Ocean Development, Technical Publication No. 13, pp 345-352 
SERUM IMMUNOGLOBULINS AND CORTISOL
DURING WINTER STAY IN ANTARCTICA:
EFFECTS OF NALTREXONE ADMINISTRATION
G. Sundaresan  and Usha Sachdeva
Department of Physiology
All India Institute of Medical Sciences
Abstract
In six volunteers, who were members of th e winter-over team of the 15 th Indian
Scientific Expedition to Antarctica, serum IgG, IgM and Cortisol were measured before and
after eight days of the opioid blocker Naltrexone (NLT) administration. The study was
conducted in six phases. There were no significant changes in the IgG levels before and after
NLT administration. However NLT administration reversed the decrease in IgM found
during the early winter and in the summer phase at the end of the isolation period indicating
a role for the opioid receptors. Results of the s erum Cortisol values measured before and
after NLT administration indicate that the central opioid receptor regulation may vary in
humans during different seasons in Antarctica. This may indeed reflect an inherent mecha-
nism involving opioids in providing adaptation to the stressful situation by taking anticipa-
tory cues from the environmental factors.
Introduction
In Antarctica there is extreme cold coupled with a varying photoperiodicity
with long polar days and polar nights amongst many other physical and social
stresses, which a human sojourner has to face while on duty in Antarctica.
Immunosuppression during Antarctic sojourn has been reported by many
authors (Muchmore  et al., l970;Tashpulatov  et al., 1971; Williams et al.,1986;
Muller et al., 1995a; Muller et al.,  1995b; Tingate et al., 1997). The observed
immunosuppression during Antarctic stay may be due to several factors such
as social and physical isolation,  extreme cold, alien photoperiodicity or may be
due to the compounded stress of all these factors.
Situations of isolation do play a strong role in the modulation of immune
responses. Sonnenfield et al.  (1992) found that the total number of leukocytes
stayed within the normal range over a 131-day isolation period in a cave. The
percentage of  polymorphonuclear leukocytes decreased by two-thirds, while
346 G.  Sundaresan & Usha Sachdeva 
the lymphocyte and monocyte percentage rose by a factor of two. Interferon
gamma production appeared to be high immediately prior to the isolation and
came down to normal range again after return of the subject to the usual
environment. Bortnovskii and Myznikov (1993) reported increased inflamma-
tory and infectious morbidity in submarine crew members during the post-
cruise period than during seagoing period and these morbidities was
characterized by seasonal outbreaks. Williams et al. (1986) studied the cutane-
ous cell mediated immunity Multitest in 2 Antarctic and sub-Antarctic groups
at quarterly intervals over a wintering year. While the sub-Antarctic group
showed comparable responsiveness to other healthy populations in temperate
regions, the Antarctic group exhibited decreased immune response.
It has been recognized that stress activates corticotrophin releasing factor
(CRF), leading to the secretion of adreno corticotrophic hormone (ACTH) and
beta-lipotropin/beta-endorphin from the anterior pituitary (Morley, 1981). Ani-
mal investigations indicate that physiologic stimulation of endogenous opioid
release forprolonged periods results in inhibition of the immune system (Shavit
et al, 1984; Morley et al, 1989). It is possible that the immunosuppression
seen in Antarctic conditions may be mediated through the release of endo-
genous opioids. This study is an attempt to find out the role of opioid receptors
in the modulation immune status of humans during their prolonged stay in
Antarctica.
Materials and Methods
Study Subjects 
The human subjects included in this study were all Indian, male members
of the 15th Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica who were on winter-over
assignment. The objectives of the study were briefed to all the members of the
expedition and only those who volunteered for the study were included. Out of
the 25 winter-over members a group of 6 volunteers were included in the study.
This group had a mean age of 33.51 ± 5.42 years and mean body weight 68.47
± 6.25 kg. All the subjects in the study were volunteers only. The ethical
considerations set by the Ethical Committee of All India Institute of Medical
Sciences were strictly followed. The subjects were given the freedom to drop
out at any point of the study, if they felt so.
Periods of the Study 
The study was conducted in six phases as given below:
Phase I: Basal - During onward voyage on board ship in December 1995, well
before the ship entered Antarctic waters (near equator, L/D 12:12, 24 ± 2 °C).
Serum Immunoglobulins and Cortisol during Winter Stay  347
Phase II: Early Winter - In April 1996 in Antarctica in early winter, at the
beginning of isolation
